title: Protest Movements against Colonial Rule
tagline: Peasant, tribal, worker and early nationalist protests before the arrival of Gandhi.

overview.intro: Before mass nationalism took shape, resistance to colonial rule took many local forms. Peasants resisted revenue and indigo, tribals defended their forests against exclusion, workers struck in the new mills and railways, and a generation of educated Indians built a constitutional agitation in the centres of British power. This unit examines these protest movements, their causes and their limits, so that the later Gandhian movements can be understood as a culmination rather than a beginning.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: Local, single-issue and unconnected, which is why each was contained separately by the administration.

learn.title: Peasant protest: Indigo and the Deccan

blocks.text: The Indigo revolt of 1859–60 in Bengal arose from a system in which European planters compelled cultivators to grow indigo on a fraction of their land at prices far below the market, and punished refusal with beatings and the seizure of property. When the price of indigo dyes fell with the discovery of synthetic alternatives, the planters pressed the cultivators harder rather than releasing them. The refusal to sow spread village by village, was supported by local landlords and by petitions and pamphlets in the Bengali press, and the government eventually appointed a commission whose report exposed the system. The revolt is notable for being conducted by peasants through legal petition and collective refusal rather than by armed rising.

The Deccan riots of 1875 were directed at moneylenders rather than at the state directly. In a series of bad harvests the Maratha peasantry borrowed to survive, and defaults allowed moneylenders to foreclose, often taking land that had been cultivated for generations. Villages attacked moneylenders’ houses and destroyed the bond documents that recorded the debts, and the administration restored order but also passed the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879, which restricted the power of moneylenders and protected the peasant’s holding. The riots therefore show protest producing a concrete legislative gain even while it failed as an uprising.

learn.title: Tribal protest: Santhals, Mundas and the forest laws

blocks.text: Tribal communities were affected by three colonial changes at once: the extension of revenue-paying agriculture into their lands, the arrival of moneylenders who took land for debt, and the declaration of forests as state property, which cut off the shifting cultivation, grazing and produce on which they depended. The Santhal hool of 1855–56 was an armed rising by the Santhals of the Rajmahal hills against the oppression of landlords, traders and moneylenders, and it was suppressed by troops after months of fighting, after which a separate Santhal district was created to give some protection.

Birsa Munda led the Munda uprising of 1899–1900 in the Chotanagpur region, promising the restoration of Munda rights over the forest and land and gathering a following among villages facing eviction. The movement had both a religious and a political character, and its suppression led to a change in policy rather than merely to punishment: the regulations of 1908 secured for the Mundas a recognised right over their customary lands, so the uprising is remembered as one where protest produced a lasting legal protection.

items: Forest laws turned common resources into state property without compensation.
Moneylenders converted seasonal debt into permanent loss of land.
Tribal protest combined religious renewal with claims to land rights.
Suppression was followed in two cases by administrative concession.
The Munda movement achieved a legal recognition of customary tenure.

learn.title: Workers’ protest and the rise of early nationalism

blocks.text: The growth of mills, jute works and railway workshops created an industrial working class that protested through strikes over wages, hours and dismissal. Early actions were local and short, but they demonstrated that the new workforce could withdraw its labour, and by the 1920s trade unions were being organised at a national level, with the All India Trade Union Congress founded in 1920. The administration responded with repressive laws and with conciliation, and the right to organise remained contested for decades.

Early nationalism took an institutional form with the Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, whose early leaders pursued petitions, memorials and resolutions in what is called the petitions phase. Dadabhai Naoroji’s drain theory supplied the economic critique, and by the turn of the century a more militant wing, remembered as Lal, Bal and Pal, pressed for swaraj as a birthright and for swadeshi and national education. The Surat split of 1907 divided the moderates and the extremists, and the First World War eventually brought the two strands back together under a broader mass politics.

learn.title: Strengths and limits of pre-Gandhian protest

blocks.text: The strength of the earlier movements was that they were deep in their own localities, that they drew on a wide social base, and that they repeatedly forced administrative concession: a commission on indigo, relief legislation for Deccan cultivators, a Santhal district, and tenure protection for the Mundas. Their weakness was that they were single-issue and geographically scattered, so the state could negotiate with or repress each one separately. Few of them established an enduring organisation, and the absence of a national framework meant that a victory in one region did not strengthen the next struggle elsewhere.

items: Local movements achieved real concessions but could not combine their pressure.
Single-issue protest left the wider structure of colonial rule untouched.
Tribal and peasant actions rarely linked with the educated nationalist leadership.
Working-class organisation was young and fragmented until the 1920s.
The national Congress supplied the framework that earlier protests lacked.

questions.prompt: The law passed in 1879 protecting the cultivators of the Deccan from moneylenders is the Deccan Agriculturists __________ Act.
questions.explanation: The Act restricted foreclosure and protected the peasant’s holding, a direct legislative result of the riots.

questions.prompt: The Santhal rising of 1855–56 is also known by the Santhal word for rebellion, __________ .
questions.explanation: The hool was an armed rising of the Santhals against landlords, traders and moneylenders in the Rajmahal hills.

questions.prompt: State four causes of tribal protest against colonial rule.
questions.answer: Four causes are: the declaration of forests as state property, which cut off grazing, produce and shifting cultivation; the extension of revenue agriculture onto tribal lands; moneylenders converting seasonal debt into permanent loss of land; and the disruption of traditional village authority by the new administration. Each of these removed a resource the community depended on.
questions.explanation: Each cause needs to show what resource or right was taken, since that is the mechanism of the grievance.

questions.prompt: Describe the Indigo revolt and its outcome.
questions.answer: The Indigo revolt of 1859–60 in Bengal and Bihar was a refusal by cultivators to grow indigo under contracts imposed by European planters, who forced them to take a fraction of their land at prices well below the market and punished refusal with violence. As synthetic dyes reduced the crop’s value, the planters pressed harder and the cultivators refused to sow, village by village, supported by local zamindars and by a Bengali-language press campaign that publicised the planters’ brutality. The method was collective refusal and legal petition rather than armed rising. The government appointed a commission of enquiry whose report confirmed the abuse, and the system collapsed shortly afterwards, since indigo cultivation could not survive without the coercion that had sustained it.
questions.explanation: The answer needs grievance, method, press role and outcome, because the outcome alone does not explain why it succeeded.

questions.prompt: Explain the growth of early nationalism from the founding of the Congress to the Surat split of 1907.
questions.answer: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 and its early leaders, the moderates, pursued change through petitions, memorials and annual resolutions, asking for a greater share of Indians in the legislative councils, the reduction of the home charges, protection for Indian industry and an end to the worst excesses of administrative violence. Their economic critique was sharpened by Dadabhai Naoroji’s drain theory, which gave a statistical case for the argument that India’s poverty was a product of rule rather than of conditions. By the turn of the century a younger group argued that the petitions had produced too little, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal pressed for swaraj as a birthright, for swadeshi in the wake of the partition of Bengal in 1905, and for national education and boycott. The two wings disagreed over whether the Extremists’ mass methods would strengthen or wreck the movement, and the disagreement came to a head at Surat in 1907, where the Congress split and the two groups went their separate ways for several years. The First World War and the changes it brought eventually prepared the ground for reunion at Lucknow in 1916.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the moderate phase, the extremist alternative, the content of each programme and the reason the split occurred.

questions.prompt: Compare the Indigo revolt and the Munda uprising as forms of resistance, and explain what each achieved.
questions.answer: The two movements differ in social base, method and result. The Indigo revolt was a peasant rising in a densely settled agricultural region where the grievance was a coercive crop contract imposed by European planters, and its method was collective refusal to sow supported by petitioning and by the Bengali press, which gave it a constitutional character. The Munda uprising was a tribal movement in the Chotanagpur forests where the grievance was the loss of forest and land rights to the state, landlords and moneylenders, and its method was armed rising under a leader who combined religious authority with a claim to restore Munda rule. In result, the Indigo revolt destroyed a system rather than producing a law, since the commission of enquiry exposed the coercion and the crop could not survive without it, while the Munda rising was militarily defeated but converted into the regulations of 1908, which secured customary tenure and left a durable legal protection. The comparison shows that resistance took the form the local structure allowed: where a free press existed the peasants could use it, and where land tenure was the issue only a legal concession would address it.
questions.explanation: Marks are for a structured comparison on at least three bases and a judgement about why the outcomes differed.
